title: Trees & Graphs — Structures, Traversals, and Reasoning
subtitle: 80 questions covering tree/graph fundamentals, BST, traversals, BFS/DFS, and why-questions on algorithm choices

questions.question: What is the maximum number of nodes a binary tree of height h can have?
questions.explanation: A perfect binary tree of height h has 2^0 + 2^1 + ... + 2^h = 2^(h+1) - 1 nodes. Height 0 (root only) gives 1 node = 2^1 - 1. Height h gives 2^(h+1) - 1.

questions.question: What is the minimum height of a binary tree containing n nodes?
questions.explanation: Height is minimized when the tree is as complete as possible (all levels filled except possibly the last). That gives height = floor(log2(n)). For n=7 nodes, floor(log2(7))=2, which matches a perfect tree of height 2.

questions.question: In a tree with n nodes, how many edges does it have?
questions.explanation: Every node except the root has exactly one parent edge, so the number of edges equals the number of non-root nodes = n - 1. This is a fundamental property of trees (acyclic connected graphs).

questions.question: What distinguishes a full binary tree from a complete binary tree?
options: A full binary tree has every node with exactly 0 or 2 children; a complete binary tree has all levels filled except possibly the last, filled left to right
A full binary tree has all leaves at the same depth; a complete binary tree has nodes with 0 or 2 children
A full binary tree is always balanced; a complete binary tree is never balanced
There is no distinction — both terms describe the same structure
questions.explanation: Full binary tree: every node has 0 or 2 children (no node with exactly 1 child). Complete binary tree: all levels are fully filled except possibly the last level, which is filled from left to right. A perfect binary tree satisfies both.

questions.question: What is the height of a single-node tree (root only)?
questions.explanation: Height is the number of edges on the longest path from root to a leaf. A single node has no edges below it, so height = 0. Some textbooks define height as the number of nodes on the path (giving 1), but the standard CS convention is 0 for a root-only tree.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a property of a tree?
options: It has exactly n-1 edges for n nodes
Every pair of nodes is connected by exactly two distinct paths
questions.explanation: A tree is connected, acyclic, and has n-1 edges. These three properties are equivalent definitions. Exactly two distinct paths between some pair of nodes would create a cycle, violating the tree property. In a tree, every pair of nodes has exactly one unique path.

questions.question: What is the depth of a node in a tree?
options: The number of nodes in the subtree rooted at that node
The number of edges from the root to that node
The number of children that node has
The height of the subtree rooted at that node
questions.explanation: Depth of a node = number of edges from the root to that node. The root has depth 0. Height is measured upward from leaves; depth is measured downward from the root. Subtree size is a separate concept.

questions.question: A binary tree has 15 nodes and is perfect (all leaves at the same level). What is its height?
questions.explanation: A perfect binary tree of height h has 2^(h+1) - 1 nodes. Setting 2^(h+1) - 1 = 15 gives 2^(h+1) = 16, so h+1 = 4, h = 3.

questions.question: In a binary tree, a node with no children is called a:
questions.explanation: A leaf (or external node) has no children. The root is the topmost node. Internal nodes have at least one child. Siblings are nodes sharing the same parent.

questions.question: What is the maximum number of leaves in a full binary tree with n internal nodes?
questions.explanation: In a full binary tree, the number of leaves L and internal nodes I satisfy L = I + 1. With n internal nodes, there are n+1 leaves. This can be proved by induction: each internal node contributes 2 children but uses 1 slot, net gain = 1.

questions.question: What is the BST property?
options: For every node, all values in the left subtree are greater, and all in the right subtree are smaller
For every node, all values in the left subtree are smaller, and all in the right subtree are greater
All nodes at even depth store even values and odd depth store odd values
The left and right subtrees of every node must have the same height
questions.explanation: BST invariant: for any node N, every value in N's left subtree is strictly less than N's value, and every value in N's right subtree is strictly greater. This enables O(log n) search by halving the search space at each node.

questions.question: What is the average-case time complexity of search in a BST with n nodes?
questions.explanation: In a balanced BST, search eliminates half the remaining nodes at each step, giving O(log n). However, in the worst case (a degenerate/skewed tree), search degrades to O(n). The average case assumes a reasonably balanced tree.

questions.question: In which order does an inorder traversal of a BST visit nodes?
questions.explanation: Inorder traversal (left → root → right) of a BST visits nodes in non-decreasing order because the BST property guarantees all left descendants are smaller and all right descendants are larger.

questions.question: When deleting a node with two children from a BST, which value typically replaces it?
options: The root of the left subtree
The inorder predecessor or inorder successor
The largest value in the tree
The parent of the deleted node
questions.explanation: Replacing with the inorder successor (smallest in right subtree) or inorder predecessor (largest in left subtree) maintains the BST property. Both have at most one child, simplifying their own deletion after the replacement.

questions.question: What is the worst-case time complexity of insert, delete, and search in an unbalanced BST?
questions.explanation: If nodes are inserted in sorted order (e.g., 1, 2, 3, ..., n), the BST degenerates into a linked list of height n. Every operation then traverses all n nodes in the worst case: O(n).

questions.question: Given the BST with root 10, left child 5, right child 15: is inserting 7 correct to the right of 5?
options: No, because 7 < 10, so it must go left of 10; then 7 > 5, so it goes right of 5 — this is correct
No, 7 should be inserted as the left child of 10
No, 7 should be the right child of 15
questions.explanation: Starting at root 10: 7 < 10, go left to 5. At 5: 7 > 5, go right. Since 5 has no right child, 7 is placed there. The answer confirms the insertion is correct and explains the traversal path.

questions.question: Why does an AVL tree guarantee O(log n) operations while a plain BST does not?
options: AVL trees sort elements before insertion
AVL trees maintain a balance factor of at most 1 between left and right subtree heights at every node, preventing degeneration
AVL trees use hash-based indexing for faster access
AVL trees limit the total number of nodes to log n
questions.explanation: A plain BST can degenerate to O(n) height. An AVL tree enforces |height(left) - height(right)| <= 1 at every node after each insert/delete via rotations. This keeps height at O(log n), guaranteeing O(log n) for all operations.

questions.question: What does it mean for a BST to be 'degenerate'?
options: Every node has exactly two children
The tree has become a linear chain (every node has at most one child), resembling a linked list
The tree has more leaves than internal nodes
questions.explanation: A degenerate BST occurs when insertions happen in sorted order (ascending or descending), making every node have only one child. The height becomes n-1 and operations degrade to O(n).

questions.question: What is the inorder successor of a node N in a BST?
options: The smallest node in N's right subtree
The largest node in N's left subtree
The rightmost node in the entire tree
questions.explanation: The inorder successor is the next node in sorted order. If N has a right subtree, it is the minimum (leftmost node) of that subtree. If N has no right subtree, it is the lowest ancestor for which N is in the left subtree.

questions.question: Given a BST, what is the time complexity of finding the minimum element?
options: O(h) where h is the tree height
questions.explanation: The minimum is found by following left child pointers from the root until reaching a node with no left child. This takes O(h) time. In a balanced tree h = O(log n); in a degenerate tree h = O(n).

questions.question: In inorder traversal of a binary tree, what is the visit order?
questions.explanation: Inorder: Left subtree first, then root, then right subtree. This produces sorted output for a BST. Preorder is Root→Left→Right; Postorder is Left→Right→Root.

questions.question: In preorder traversal, the root is visited at which point?
questions.explanation: Preorder: Root → Left → Right. The root is processed first (before any subtree), which is why it is called 'pre'-order. This is useful for copying a tree or serializing its structure.

questions.question: Given the tree: root=1, left=2, right=3, 2's left=4, 2's right=5. What is the inorder traversal?
questions.explanation: Inorder (L→Root→R): Visit 4, then 2, then 5 (left subtree of 1 complete), then 1 (root), then 3. Result: 4, 2, 5, 1, 3.

questions.question: Given the same tree (root=1, left=2, right=3, 2's children=4,5), what is the preorder traversal?
questions.explanation: Preorder (Root→L→R): Visit 1, then recurse left: 2, then 4, then 5, then recurse right: 3. Result: 1, 2, 4, 5, 3.

questions.question: Given the same tree (root=1, left=2, right=3, 2's children=4,5), what is the postorder traversal?
questions.explanation: Postorder (L→R→Root): Visit 4, then 5, then 2 (left subtree done), then 3 (right subtree done), then 1 (root). Result: 4, 5, 2, 3, 1.

questions.question: Which traversal visits nodes level by level from top to bottom, left to right?
questions.explanation: Level-order traversal uses a queue and visits all nodes at depth d before any node at depth d+1, going left to right within each level. It is equivalent to BFS on the tree.

questions.question: Which traversal is used to delete a binary tree node-by-node without violating memory safety?
questions.explanation: Postorder deletes children before their parent. If the parent were deleted first (preorder), the children would become orphaned and their memory leaked. Postorder ensures children are freed before the parent.

questions.question: Which traversal produces a copy of a tree with the same structural order?
questions.explanation: Preorder (Root→L→R) creates the root first, then its left subtree, then right — the same order needed to rebuild the tree. If you serialize with preorder and deserialize in the same order, the structure is reproduced. Inorder alone is insufficient to reconstruct a tree uniquely.

questions.question: Given preorder = [3,9,20,15,7] and inorder = [9,3,15,20,7], what is the root's right child?
questions.explanation: The first element in preorder is the root: 3. In inorder, 3 splits [9] (left) and [15,20,7] (right). The right subtree's preorder is [20,15,7], so the right child of 3 is 20.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of any DFS-based tree traversal (inorder, preorder, postorder)?
questions.explanation: Every node is visited exactly once in any DFS traversal, regardless of tree shape. The total work is O(n). O(h) describes the stack depth (space), not the time to visit all nodes.

questions.question: What is the space complexity of recursive inorder traversal on a balanced binary tree?
questions.explanation: Recursive traversal uses the call stack, which goes as deep as the tree height. For a balanced tree, height = O(log n), so space = O(log n). For a skewed tree it would be O(n).

questions.question: Which data structure is used to implement iterative inorder traversal?
questions.explanation: Iterative inorder traversal simulates the recursive call stack explicitly using a stack. The algorithm pushes left children until reaching null, then pops and visits, then moves to the right child.

questions.question: In a Morris traversal, what mechanism allows inorder traversal in O(1) extra space?
options: A hash map stores visited nodes
Temporary right-child pointers (threads) are created to link nodes back to their inorder successors
The tree is converted to an array before traversal
A global pointer tracks the current position
questions.explanation: Morris traversal temporarily modifies the tree by threading the rightmost node of a left subtree back to its inorder successor. This allows returning from a left subtree without a stack or recursion, then removing the thread before moving right. Space is O(1).

questions.question: When reconstructing a binary tree, which pair of traversals is sufficient to uniquely determine the tree?
questions.explanation: Inorder paired with preorder, or inorder paired with postorder, uniquely reconstructs any binary tree (assuming no duplicate values). Preorder + postorder alone is insufficient — multiple trees can share the same preorder and postorder sequences.

questions.question: What is the output of level-order traversal on a tree with root=5, left=3, right=7, 3's children=2,4, 7's right=9?
questions.explanation: Level 0: 5. Level 1: 3, 7. Level 2: 2, 4 (children of 3), 9 (right child of 7). Result: 5, 3, 7, 2, 4, 9.

questions.question: Why is postorder traversal used for evaluating expression trees?
options: Because operators must be printed before their operands
Because an operator can only be applied after both operand subtrees have been evaluated
Because expression trees must be traversed in sorted order
Because level-order evaluation requires more memory
questions.explanation: In an expression tree, internal nodes are operators and leaves are operands. Postorder visits left subtree (evaluates left operand), then right subtree (evaluates right operand), then root (applies the operator). The operator must come last — it cannot be applied before its operands are known.

questions.question: Which traversal is equivalent to reading a tree's nodes in 'reverse postorder' and is used in topological sort with DFS?
questions.explanation: In DFS-based topological sort on a DAG, nodes are pushed onto a stack after all their descendants are fully explored (postorder). Reading the stack in reverse gives a valid topological order — this is reverse postorder.

questions.question: What is the relationship between inorder traversal of a BST and a sorted array?
options: Inorder traversal produces elements in reverse sorted order
Inorder traversal produces elements in non-decreasing (sorted ascending) order
Inorder traversal produces elements in insertion order
Inorder traversal and sorted order are unrelated
questions.explanation: By the BST invariant, inorder (left→root→right) visits smaller elements before larger ones at every node, producing a globally sorted sequence. This property is why BST inorder traversal is used to implement sorted iteration.

questions.question: What is the difference between a directed and an undirected graph?
options: Directed graphs can have cycles; undirected graphs cannot
In a directed graph, edges have a direction (from→to); in an undirected graph, edges are bidirectional
Directed graphs always have more edges than undirected graphs
questions.explanation: A directed graph (digraph) has ordered pairs (u,v) as edges: going from u to v does not imply going from v to u. An undirected graph treats (u,v) and (v,u) as the same edge. Both can have cycles.

questions.question: What is the maximum number of edges in a simple undirected graph with n vertices?
questions.explanation: In a simple graph (no self-loops, no parallel edges), each pair of vertices can have at most one edge. The number of pairs of n vertices is C(n,2) = n(n-1)/2. This is achieved by the complete graph K_n.

questions.question: What is the difference between an adjacency matrix and an adjacency list representation?
options: An adjacency matrix stores edge weights; an adjacency list stores only connectivity
An adjacency matrix uses O(V^2) space; an adjacency list uses O(V + E) space
An adjacency matrix is for undirected graphs only; adjacency list is for directed graphs
An adjacency matrix is faster for all operations than an adjacency list
questions.explanation: Adjacency matrix: V×V grid, O(V^2) space, O(1) edge lookup. Adjacency list: array of lists, O(V+E) space, O(degree) edge lookup. For sparse graphs (E << V^2), adjacency list is more space-efficient. Both support weighted graphs.

questions.question: What is the in-degree of a vertex in a directed graph?
options: The number of edges leaving that vertex
The number of edges entering that vertex
The total number of edges incident to that vertex
The number of vertices reachable from that vertex
questions.explanation: In a directed graph, in-degree = number of incoming edges. Out-degree = number of outgoing edges. For undirected graphs, there is only 'degree' (total incident edges). Sum of all in-degrees equals the number of edges.

questions.question: What is a DAG?
options: A graph where all vertices have the same degree
A directed graph with no directed cycles
A graph where every vertex is reachable from every other vertex
A graph with no parallel edges
questions.explanation: DAG = Directed Acyclic Graph. It has directed edges but no directed cycle (no path from a vertex back to itself). DAGs are the foundation for topological sort and model dependencies, task scheduling, and compiler data flow.

questions.question: In a connected undirected graph with V vertices and E edges, what additional constraint makes it a tree?
questions.explanation: A connected acyclic undirected graph (tree) always has exactly E = V - 1 edges. Adding one more edge creates a cycle; removing one disconnects the graph.

questions.question: What is a strongly connected component (SCC) in a directed graph?
options: A subgraph where every vertex has the same out-degree
A maximal subgraph where every vertex is reachable from every other vertex via directed paths
A subgraph with no directed edges
The largest clique in the graph
questions.explanation: An SCC is a maximal set of vertices such that there is a directed path from every vertex to every other vertex within the set. Kosaraju's and Tarjan's algorithms find all SCCs in O(V+E).

questions.question: Which graph representation is preferred for dense graphs and why?
options: Adjacency list — because it uses less memory for dense graphs
Adjacency matrix — because O(1) edge lookup pays off when E is close to V^2
Edge list — because iteration over all edges is fastest
Adjacency matrix — because it supports negative weights
questions.explanation: For dense graphs (E ≈ V^2), an adjacency matrix wastes little relative space and its O(1) edge-existence check is advantageous. An adjacency list's O(degree) lookup becomes expensive when degrees are high. For sparse graphs, the list is better.

questions.question: What does BFS on an unweighted graph guarantee about the paths it finds?
options: The paths have the minimum total weight
The paths have the minimum number of edges (shortest path by hop count)
The paths visit every vertex exactly once
The paths are found in O(log V) time
questions.explanation: BFS explores vertices in order of their distance (number of edges) from the source. The first time a vertex is reached, it is via the shortest path by hop count. This does NOT account for edge weights — for weighted shortest paths, Dijkstra's algorithm is needed.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of BFS on a graph with V vertices and E edges using an adjacency list?
questions.explanation: BFS visits each vertex once (O(V)) and processes each edge once when scanning adjacency lists (O(E)), giving O(V + E) total. With an adjacency matrix the edge scanning cost is O(V^2).

questions.question: In BFS, what data structure is used to track the frontier (vertices to be processed next)?
questions.explanation: BFS uses a FIFO queue. Discovered vertices are enqueued; the next vertex to process is always dequeued from the front. This ensures vertices are explored in non-decreasing distance order from the source.

questions.question: In DFS, when is a vertex's discovery time and finish time recorded, and what do they represent?
options: Discovery = when enqueued; finish = when dequeued
Discovery = when first visited; finish = when all descendants have been fully explored
Discovery = when added to visited set; finish = when neighbors are scanned
Both are recorded only in topological sort, not general DFS
questions.explanation: In DFS with timestamps: discovery time d[v] is set when v is first encountered (gray); finish time f[v] is set when v's entire subtree has been explored (black). These timestamps reveal parenthesis structure, cycle detection, and SCC membership.

questions.question: What type of edge in DFS indicates a cycle in a directed graph?
questions.explanation: A back edge connects a vertex to one of its ancestors in the DFS tree — meaning there is a path from the ancestor down to the current node, and the back edge completes a cycle. No back edge = no directed cycle = DAG.

questions.question: Why does DFS use a stack (or recursion) while BFS uses a queue?
options: DFS needs to remember visited nodes; BFS does not
DFS explores as deep as possible before backtracking (LIFO), while BFS explores all neighbors at the current level before going deeper (FIFO)
DFS requires random access to vertices; BFS does not
DFS is faster than BFS, which is why a stack is used
questions.explanation: DFS goes deep first: when a neighbor is discovered, it is immediately explored recursively (LIFO — last discovered, first explored). BFS spreads outward level by level: all neighbors of the current node are queued for later (FIFO — first discovered, first explored). The data structure directly encodes the exploration order.

questions.question: BFS on a graph starting from vertex A visits: A, B, C, D, E in that order. If the adjacency list of A is [B, C] and B's is [D, E], which vertex is visited 4th?
questions.explanation: BFS queue starts with A. Dequeue A, enqueue B and C → queue: [B,C]. Dequeue B (2nd visited), enqueue D and E → queue: [C,D,E]. Dequeue C (3rd visited). Dequeue D — D is visited 4th.

questions.question: What is the space complexity of BFS in the worst case?
questions.explanation: BFS holds at most one full level of the graph in its queue. In the worst case (a star graph), all V-1 leaves are discovered at once, requiring O(V) queue space. The visited array also uses O(V).

questions.question: Which algorithm finds all connected components in an undirected graph by running DFS/BFS from each unvisited vertex?
options: A modified DFS/BFS that labels each vertex with its component ID
questions.explanation: Running DFS or BFS from every unvisited vertex marks all reachable vertices with the same component label. Each new DFS/BFS start indicates a new component. Total time is O(V+E). Dijkstra and Kruskal solve different problems.

questions.question: In DFS of an undirected graph, which type of edge does NOT exist (unlike in directed graphs)?
options: Cross edge is impossible but forward/cross edges merge
questions.explanation: In undirected DFS, every non-tree edge is a back edge (to an ancestor). Forward edges and cross edges do not exist in undirected DFS because an edge to a descendant or to a vertex in a different branch would already have been a tree edge or back edge from the other direction.

questions.question: What does DFS on a DAG produce that BFS cannot directly?
options: Shortest paths between all pairs of vertices
questions.explanation: DFS-based topological sort uses finish times: vertices are added to a result list in decreasing finish time order. BFS does not naturally produce finish times or topological ordering. BFS produces shortest paths; MST uses Prim's/Kruskal's.

questions.question: When is BFS preferred over DFS for pathfinding?
options: When the graph has many cycles
When the shortest path by number of edges is needed in an unweighted graph
questions.explanation: BFS guarantees the shortest path (minimum edges) in unweighted graphs because it explores vertices in non-decreasing hop distance. DFS may find a path but not the shortest one. For weighted shortest paths, Dijkstra's algorithm is used.

questions.question: Why does DFS naturally solve the problem of detecting whether a directed graph is a DAG?
options: Because DFS visits vertices in topological order
Because the presence of a back edge in DFS is both necessary and sufficient for the existence of a directed cycle
Because DFS runs in O(V) time, which is fast enough for cycle detection
Because DFS always terminates before BFS
questions.explanation: A directed graph is a DAG if and only if DFS finds no back edges. A back edge (u,v) where v is an ancestor of u implies a cycle v→...→u→v. If there is a cycle, DFS will encounter a gray ancestor and produce a back edge. This equivalence makes DFS the canonical cycle-detection tool.

questions.question: Given an unweighted graph, if BFS from source S reaches vertex T after processing 3 levels, what is the shortest path length from S to T?
questions.explanation: BFS processes level 0 (S itself), level 1 (neighbors of S), level 2, level 3, etc. If T is first reached at level 3, the shortest path is exactly 3 edges. BFS guarantees this is the minimum.

questions.question: Why is a queue (not a stack) essential for BFS to guarantee shortest paths?
options: Because a queue is faster than a stack for this workload
Because FIFO ordering ensures vertices are explored in non-decreasing distance order, so the first time a vertex is reached, it is via the shortest path
Because a stack would cause infinite loops in cyclic graphs
Because a queue supports more efficient memory allocation
questions.explanation: With a FIFO queue, all vertices at distance d are dequeued before any vertex at distance d+1. The first time vertex T is dequeued, no shorter path can exist — all shorter-path candidates were already processed. A stack (LIFO) would explore a deep path before shallower ones, reaching T via a potentially longer route first.

questions.question: Why must topological sort be performed only on DAGs?
options: Because DAGs have fewer vertices than cyclic graphs
Because a cycle creates a circular dependency — no valid linear ordering exists where every edge points forward
Because DFS cannot run on graphs with cycles
Because topological sort requires edge weights, which DAGs always have
questions.explanation: Topological ordering requires that for every edge (u,v), u appears before v. A cycle A→B→C→A means A must precede B, B precede C, and C precede A — a contradiction. DAGs, having no cycles, always admit at least one valid topological ordering.

questions.question: Why is Dijkstra's algorithm incorrect when graphs contain negative edge weights?
options: Because Dijkstra's algorithm does not handle weighted graphs
Because a previously finalized vertex could be reached by a shorter path through a later-discovered negative edge, violating the greedy assumption
Because negative weights cause integer overflow
Because Dijkstra's algorithm only works on directed graphs
questions.explanation: Dijkstra's greedy assumption: once a vertex is extracted from the priority queue with distance d, d is final. With negative edges, a later path via a negative edge could yield a shorter distance to an already-finalized vertex. Bellman-Ford handles negative weights by relaxing all edges V-1 times.

questions.question: Why does Kruskal's algorithm sort edges by weight before processing?
options: To process all edges in a fixed time regardless of graph size
To greedily add the globally cheapest edge that does not form a cycle, guaranteeing a minimum spanning tree
To ensure edges are added in topological order
To avoid visiting the same vertex twice
questions.explanation: Kruskal's builds an MST by repeatedly picking the minimum-weight edge that connects two different components (does not form a cycle). Sorting ensures the cheapest available edge is always processed next. Skipping any cheaper edge would risk a non-minimum spanning tree.

questions.question: Why is an adjacency list preferred over an adjacency matrix for BFS/DFS on sparse graphs?
options: Because the adjacency list supports O(1) edge lookup
Because iterating over a vertex's neighbors in an adjacency list takes O(degree) time, whereas in a matrix it takes O(V) — wasteful when degree is small
Because adjacency lists are simpler to implement
Because adjacency matrices do not support directed graphs
questions.explanation: BFS/DFS visits each edge once. With an adjacency list, scanning all neighbors of a vertex costs O(degree). With a matrix, scanning the entire row costs O(V) even if the vertex has only 2 neighbors. For sparse graphs (E << V^2), this difference compounds to O(V+E) vs O(V^2) total.

questions.question: Why does Prim's algorithm use a min-priority queue?
options: To sort all edges before processing
To always extend the current MST by the minimum-weight edge crossing the cut between tree and non-tree vertices
To detect cycles during MST construction
To process vertices in BFS order
questions.explanation: Prim's maintains the invariant that at each step, the cheapest edge from the current tree to an unvisited vertex is chosen. A min-priority queue (min-heap) allows extracting this minimum-cost edge in O(log V) rather than O(V) by linear scan.

questions.question: Why is a binary heap the standard backing structure for a priority queue used in Dijkstra's algorithm?
options: Because a heap provides O(1) insert and O(1) extract-min
Because a heap provides O(log V) insert and O(log V) extract-min, balancing both operations for the V extractions and E relaxations needed
Because a heap uses less memory than a sorted array
Because a heap supports random access in O(1)
questions.explanation: Dijkstra performs V extract-min and up to E decrease-key operations. A binary heap gives O(log V) for both, giving total O((V+E) log V). A sorted array would give O(1) extract-min but O(V) insert/decrease-key, which is worse for dense graphs. A Fibonacci heap gives O(log V) extract-min and O(1) amortized decrease-key, optimal for dense graphs.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of Dijkstra's algorithm with a binary min-heap on a graph with V vertices and E edges?
questions.explanation: Each vertex is extracted from the heap once: V × O(log V). Each edge may trigger a decrease-key: E × O(log V). Total: O((V + E) log V). For dense graphs (E ≈ V^2), this simplifies to O(V^2 log V); a plain array gives O(V^2) which is better for dense cases.

questions.question: Kahn's algorithm for topological sort uses in-degrees. What is the initial queue contents?
options: The vertex with the maximum in-degree
questions.explanation: Kahn's algorithm starts by enqueuing all vertices with in-degree 0 (no prerequisites). Each time a vertex is dequeued and processed, its neighbors' in-degrees are decremented; neighbors reaching in-degree 0 are enqueued. If not all vertices are processed, a cycle exists.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of topological sort (both Kahn's BFS-based and DFS-based)?
questions.explanation: Both approaches visit every vertex once and process every edge once: O(V + E). Kahn's dequeues each vertex and scans its adjacency list; DFS-based finishes each vertex once and adds it to the result.

questions.question: What is a minimum spanning tree (MST) of a connected weighted undirected graph?
options: The subgraph with minimum number of vertices connecting all edges
A spanning tree (connecting all vertices with V-1 edges, no cycles) with minimum total edge weight
The shortest path tree from a source vertex
A tree with maximum depth and minimum edge count
questions.explanation: An MST spans all V vertices with exactly V-1 edges (tree property), contains no cycles, and minimizes the sum of edge weights. It differs from shortest path trees, which optimize paths from a single source rather than total tree weight.

questions.question: In a heap represented as an array with 1-based indexing, what are the indices of the children of node at index i?
questions.explanation: For 1-based array representation of a binary heap: left child of i is at 2i, right child at 2i+1, parent at floor(i/2). For 0-based: left child at 2i+1, right at 2i+2, parent at floor((i-1)/2).

questions.question: What property does a max-heap maintain that makes it suitable as a priority queue for maximum-priority extraction?
options: Every node's value is less than its children
Every node's value is greater than or equal to its children's values
All leaves are at the same depth
The left subtree is always larger than the right subtree
questions.explanation: Max-heap property: every node ≥ its children. This guarantees the maximum element is always at the root, allowing O(1) extraction of the maximum and O(log n) re-heapification after removal.

questions.question: Bellman-Ford performs V-1 relaxation passes over all edges. Why V-1 and not V?
options: Because V-1 relaxations match the number of edges in a spanning tree
Because the shortest path in a graph with V vertices uses at most V-1 edges, so V-1 rounds guarantee convergence for all simple paths
Because the algorithm terminates early if no changes occur in a round
Because V relaxations would double-count the source vertex
questions.explanation: A shortest path visiting V vertices uses at most V-1 edges (a simple path has no repeated vertex). After k relaxation rounds, Bellman-Ford has found the correct shortest paths using at most k edges. After V-1 rounds, all shortest paths (which are simple in a graph without negative cycles) are found.

questions.question: How does Bellman-Ford detect negative-weight cycles?
options: By checking if any vertex has negative in-degree
By running a V-th relaxation pass: if any distance is updated, a negative cycle exists
By checking if the graph is a DAG
By comparing edge weights to the average edge weight
questions.explanation: After V-1 rounds, all shortest paths without negative cycles are finalized. If a V-th relaxation still reduces some distance, it means there is a path with a negative cycle that keeps decreasing — a negative cycle is detected.

questions.question: Why does a recursive DFS on a very deep graph risk stack overflow?
options: Because DFS allocates a new array for each visited vertex
Because each recursive call adds a frame to the call stack; a path of length n causes n nested frames, which can exhaust stack memory
Because DFS visits each vertex multiple times
Because the recursion depth is bounded by the number of edges, not vertices
questions.explanation: Each DFS recursive call for a deeper vertex pushes a new stack frame. For a path graph of n vertices, the recursion depth is n. Most systems have a stack limit of a few thousand to tens of thousands of frames. An iterative DFS with an explicit stack avoids this limitation.

questions.question: Which graph algorithm would correctly find the shortest path in a graph where all edge weights are equal?
options: Both BFS and Dijkstra's algorithm give correct results, but BFS is more efficient
questions.explanation: When all edge weights are equal, path length by hop count equals path length by weight. BFS finds shortest paths by hop count in O(V+E). Dijkstra also works correctly but uses a priority queue unnecessarily, giving O((V+E) log V). BFS is strictly more efficient here.

questions.question: A graph has 5 vertices and 4 edges and is connected. What kind of graph must it be?
questions.explanation: A connected graph with V vertices and exactly V-1 edges has no cycles and is by definition a tree. 5 vertices, 4 edges, connected → tree.

questions.question: Which traversal order correctly reconstructs a binary tree if given alongside the inorder sequence?
options: Either preorder or postorder, combined with inorder
Any two traversals from {inorder, preorder, postorder} are always sufficient
questions.explanation: Inorder + preorder or inorder + postorder uniquely reconstruct a binary tree (with distinct values). Preorder + postorder together are insufficient — the inorder sequence is needed to determine left/right split. Level-order alone is also insufficient.
